title: Latency Envelope Controller — adaptive admission with jitter‑dampened batch shaping
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Introduce a Latency Envelope Controller (LEC) in the serving runtime to actively shape admission and batching behavior based on a programmable latency envelope. The goal is to reduce tail latency spikes during bursty traffic and long‑sequence prefill storms while preserving throughput and keeping kernel selection optimal for the shaped batches. LEC will sit between the frontdoor admission layer and the prefill scheduler and provide: adaptive admission crediting, jitter‑dampening for microbursts, batch shape hints for kernel selector, and emergency decode rescheduling to keep latency within the envelope.
acceptance_criteria: Average 99th percentile latency for mixed small/long prompt workload reduced by at least 25% under synthetic microburst scenarios
No more than 5% throughput regression on steady-state token throughput for the tested models (70B / 13B variants)
Kernel selector receives batch shape hints and applies preferred kernel path at least 90% of the time for matching shapes
Feature flag rollout control exists in runtime and can be toggled per-tenant
Automated canary runs with production traffic sample demonstrate envelope stability for 48 hours
implementation_plan: 1) Design LEC control API and envelope DSL for SLOs (latency targets, burst budget, jitter hysteresis)
2) Implement admission credit tracker that accounts for per-tenant burst tokens and request deadlines
3) Add jitter‑dampening window that coalesces sub-50ms microbursts into controlled admission pulses
4) Add batch shape hint headers to prefill scheduler so kernel selector can prefer narrow/wide kernels
5) Implement decode emergency rescheduling to preempt long-running decodes for top-priority requests when envelope breached
6) Integrate telemetry: per-tenant envelope breaches, admission events, kernel hint success rate
7) Run canary on dedicated pool, iterate on tunables, and roll out via runtime feature flag
tasks: Design envelope DSL and default profiles (Aisha)
Batch shape hint header + scheduler consumer (Priya)
End-to-end test harness for microbursts (SRE team)
Dashboards and alerting for envelope breach (Observability)
Canary rollout and smoke test runbook (Ops)
Performance validation and compare against baseline (Benchmarking)
risks: Over‑aggressive damping may increase perceived latency for interactive small prompts
Kernel selector may not have sufficient variants to honor batch shape hints for all models
Decode preemption can cause quality regressions or partial outputs if not correctly rolled back
Per-tenant tuning complexity could require significant ops exposure and defaults may not fit all workloads
